item.title: Timeline, ethics cloud Jamaat MP’s marriage claim
item.description:
Questions over the age of a young woman, conflicting documents about her marital status, a reported recommendation for a government job and broader ethical concerns have overshadowed Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami MP Gazi Nazrul Islam’s claim that the woman seen in a viral video is his legally married second wife, placing both the lawmaker and his party under intense public scrutiny.
What began as a controversy over leaked footage of the Satkhira-4 MP has rapidly evolved into a debate over whether a public representative exercised appropriate judgment in developing a relationship with a young woman who reportedly sought his recommendation for employment, whether the timeline of their claimed marriage matches available documents, and how Jamaat -- known for its conservative moral positions -- will respond to the first major personal controversy involving one of its lawmakers.
The controversy erupted after CCTV footage showing Gazi Nazrul Islam in an intimate setting with a young woman spread widely across social media and messaging platforms.
Fact-checking organization Rumor Scanner said its technical review found no indication that the footage had been created or manipulated using artificial intelligence, helping shift public attention from the authenticity of the video to the identities of those involved and the circumstances surrounding the relationship.
Within hours of the footage going viral, the MP issued a detailed statement rejecting suggestions that it showed an extramarital relationship.
He said the woman was his second wife, Mariam Begum, and claimed they had married on June 17 in the presence of both families and with the consent of his first wife.
He described the video as private footage of a husband and wife that had been secretly recorded and later circulated as part of an extortion attempt and a politically motivated campaign to damage his reputation.
However, rather than ending the controversy, the statement prompted new questions after documents attributed to the young woman began circulating online.
One such document, described as her biodata, reportedly lists her marital status as “single” and bears what appears to be a handwritten recommendation from Gazi Nazrul Islam dated June 22, five days after the MP says they were married.
The authenticity of the biodata has not been independently verified, and neither the MP nor the woman’s family has publicly addressed the apparent discrepancy.
The same document reportedly states that the young woman was born on May 22, 2008.
If that information is accurate, she would have turned 18 before the claimed marriage on June 17, meaning she would not have been a minor under Bangladeshi law at the time of the marriage.
That has shifted public debate away from allegations of child marriage and toward broader ethical questions surrounding the relationship.
Several media reports cited in the material say the woman had been seeking government employment and that Gazi Nazrul Islam had recommended her application shortly before or around the time of the claimed marriage.
If accurate, critics argue, the issue extends beyond a private relationship and raises questions about the power imbalance between an elected lawmaker and a young job seeker seeking his support.
Rights advocates and commentators quoted in media reports have questioned whether genuine consent can be separated from influence where one individual holds political authority and the other is dependent on that authority for career opportunities.
Although no evidence has yet emerged that any law was broken in relation to the recommendation itself, the reported circumstances have intensified public debate over ethical standards expected of elected representatives.
Nazrul Islam has rejected those suggestions.
According to his account, he travelled to a business office in Dhaka’s Moghbazar on July 13 with both his first and second wives.
While they were inside, he alleged that his driver and the maternal uncle of his second wife entered the room with several unidentified individuals, held them hostage, extorted Tk1 lakh and later demanded additional money.
He claimed those involved secretly recorded private moments between him and his wife before releasing the footage online after he refused to comply with further financial demands.
He also alleged that the incident stemmed from an existing family dispute involving his second wife’s relatives and insisted the footage had been deliberately portrayed as evidence of an illicit affair to damage both his personal reputation and that of Jamaat-e-Islami.
The MP’s version has been publicly supported by his first wife, who issued a video statement confirming that he had married Mariam and warning against what she described as defamatory allegations.
The young woman also appeared in a separate video identifying herself as Nazrul Islam’s wife and saying their marriage took place on June 17 with the knowledge of both families and the presence of the MP’s first wife.
Even so, questions remain unresolved.
If the marriage took place on June 17, observers have asked why documents reportedly prepared several days later still identified the woman as single.
Likewise, no official marriage registration or other documentary evidence has yet been made public to reconcile the conflicting claims.
The controversy has also placed Jamaat-e-Islami in an uncomfortable position.
The party has said it is monitoring developments and gathering information before deciding whether any organizational action is necessary.
Assistant Secretary General Ehsanul Mahbub Zubair said the party had reviewed media reports as well as statements from the MP, his first wife, second wife and her father and would act after establishing the facts.
While some district-level leaders have publicly echoed the MP’s explanation, the party’s central leadership has stopped short of endorsing his account, indicating that it wants to examine both the legal status of the marriage and the broader political implications before reaching a decision.
Political analysts say the case presents Jamaat with one of its first major ethical tests since returning to parliamentary politics.
A failure to act decisively could expose the party to accusations of applying different standards to its own leaders, while strong disciplinary measures against one of its MPs could carry political costs of their own.
For now, the controversy remains defined less by the leaked footage than by the unanswered questions it has generated: whether the documented timeline of the marriage can be substantiated, whether the relationship created an ethical conflict for an elected representative, and whether Jamaat’s internal inquiry will satisfy growing public demands for transparency and accountability.

Trump says US 'not finished' as Iran widens attacks
item.description:
President Donald Trump warned that the United States was "not finished" attacking Iran as strikes continued Tuesday, as Tehran broadened its offensive against Gulf states after its Houthi allies threatened to blockade Saudi ports.

Two weeks after fighting resumed between the decades-old foes, Trump said Iran would need more than 20 years to recover from the damage inflicted in the Middle East war.

"If we left right now, it would take Iran 20, 25 years to rebuild," he said. "We're not finished at all...we're not leaving right now."

The US military said it had completed an 11th consecutive night of strikes against Iran, saying it targeted military infrastructure to "further degrade Iran's ability to threaten commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump also said the next US military target could be an underground complex known as Pickaxe Mountain, a subterranean nuclear site near Natanz where Western intelligence suspects Iran is building an undeclared enrichment facility.

"We'll be hitting that area pretty soon, and very heavily," Trump said, adding that he would not normally announce targets but "there's not a thing they can do about it".

Iran threatened reprisal, with the Khatam Al-Anbiya military command saying it would "consider it as an expansion of war in the region" if such an attack were carried out, threatening strikes on "all the interests of America, the allies and supporters", state-run broadcaster IRIB reported.

Bahrain meanwhile said it intercepted Iranian attacks as sirens sounded repeatedly, while Kuwait and Jordan said they had intercepted drone and missile strikes.

Kuwait's army said Wednesday morning its air defences were engaging with drone attacks from Iran.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards confirmed a strike on Jordan, saying they had targeted a "complex housing US terrorist forces in the region of Rukban".

The Iranian army had earlier said it targeted US assets in Kuwait and Bahrain, including air defence systems, radar installations and administrative buildings.

"With this radar sweep, the enemy should prepare for even more decisive and powerful waves of drone and missile attacks," the Guards said in a statement carried by state news agency IRNA.

Houthi threat

Trump said he would "take care of" Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels if they followed through on a threat Monday to blockade Saudi Arabia's ports.

"If something like that happens, we take care of it," Trump said. "We've done that with the Houthis before, and we haven't heard from them in a while since we did what we did originally."

Saudi Arabia strongly condemned the threat from what it called the "terrorist Houthi militia".

It remains unclear how the Houthis would enforce such a blockade.

But maritime intelligence provider Vanguard Tech said a Singapore-flagged tanker and a Liberia-flagged tanker both "reversed course" in the Red Sea after loading crude at the Saudi port of Yanbu.

If the Houthis make good on the threat, they could endanger Riyadh's ability to bypass the Strait of Hormuz for some oil exports, with major repercussions for the global economy.

Saudi Arabia and the Houthis traded fire last week for the first time in years, threatening a 2022 truce, but the rebels have largely remained on the sidelines since Israel and the United States attacked Iran in late February.

The Revolutionary Guards said Tuesday that two tankers attempting to transit the strait "were hit by explosions, resulting in massive fires that brought them to a standstill".

The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency earlier reported that an "unknown projectile" struck a tanker off the coast of Oman.

Cost of war

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told US senators Tuesday that the war has cost the United States $37.5 billion so far, up from a previous estimate of nearly $29 billion in mid-May.

In Iran, Shahin, a 34-year-old embroiderer from Iranshahr, said: "We're still struggling to secure our most basic life necessities, and now we're dealing with destruction from the war on top of it."

Despite the fighting, Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said diplomatic exchanges with Washington through mediators were continuing.

Mediator Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif called for restraint during a meeting with Iran's Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni.

Sharif urged all sides to "refrain from actions that could further destabilise the region", his office said.

item.title: Allowing Iran control of Hormuz "dangerous precedent", Rubio tells ASEAN
item.description:
PHILIPPINES-ASEAN

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Southeast Asian foreign ministers on Wednesday that Iranian control of the Strait of Hormuz would set a dangerous precedent with repercussions beyond the Middle East.

His comments came as US Central Command said it had begun striking military targets in Iran for the "11th consecutive night" in a bid to degrade the country's ability to threaten commercial shipping in the waterway.

"If we create a precedent in the Middle East where a nation-state can decide to control an international waterway, charge a toll, and blow up your ships if you don't pay, we have created a very dangerous precedent that will repeat itself in other parts of the world, including this region," Rubio told envoys at a Manila gathering of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).

"At its core, it's very simple. Iran demands the right -- which they do not have under any existing legal mechanism -- to control the transit of traffic through the Strait of Hormuz," he said.

"There is a fundamental principle about freedom of navigation that is threatened," he added.

"That cannot be allowed to happen."

Rubio's remarks came as the region is grappling with a series of overlapping claims by China and ASEAN member states in the South China Sea, another crucial maritime route for global trade.

His arrival in the Philippines on Tuesday morning coincided with the US condemnation of a recent clash between Chinese and Philippine sailors in the disputed waterway.

Rubio is to meet his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi on Wednesday on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit, where he will also have talks with fellow Quad members India, Australia and Japan, and others.

The secretary of state added that the United States remains "open" to diplomacy with Iran but that Tehran is not "serious".

"The United States remains open and willing to engage in positive and constructive negotiations and discussions, provided that the commitments made are honored," he said.

"The problem we are currently facing is that they are not taking the negotiations seriously," Rubio said.

"If they are serious, we will be too. If they are not, then we will do what is necessary to protect our interests and those of our allies."

item.title: Why Delhi's streets tell a bigger democratic story
item.description:
Politics has never depended solely on votes, parliamentary arithmetic, or ideological conviction. It has always depended on stories that societies tell about themselves.
Every government seeks to define what counts as patriotism, dissent, responsibility, and disorder. Every protest movement attempts to rewrite those definitions.
The confrontation that unfolded on the streets of New Delhi during the "Sangsad Chalo" march was therefore about far more than examination paper leaks or the resignation of a cabinet minister.
It revealed an increasingly visible struggle over who possesses the authority to shape political legitimacy in the world's largest democracy.
The immediate trigger appeared familiar. Allegations of repeated examination irregularities, frustrations over unemployment, and accusations of administrative negligence brought thousands of young people to the capital.
Such grievances are hardly unique to India. Across South Asia, public examinations have become gateways to shrinking opportunities rather than pathways to social mobility.
When those gateways are compromised by corruption or incompetence, the consequences extend well beyond disappointed candidates. Faith in merit itself begins to erode.
Yet what distinguished Delhi's protests was not simply the anger of students. It was the remarkable transformation of language surrounding the movement.
A label that had reportedly been intended as an insult evolved into the name of a movement that many participants embraced with unmistakable irony.
The so-called Cockroach Janata Party became more than an online joke. It illustrated how digital political culture increasingly allows citizens to neutrali z e ridicule by appropriating it.
This reversal deserves closer attention because it represents one of the defining characteristics of contemporary politics.
Throughout much of the 20th century, political elites possessed significant control over public narratives. Governments issued statements, newspapers interpreted them, and opposition parties attempted to respond through speeches or organised demonstrations.
Today, however, political communication travels through an entirely different ecosystem. Every slogan is instantly dissected, remixed, parodied, and redistributed by millions of users before official explanations can even catch up.
The Delhi protests demonstrated this transformation with remarkable clarity. Instead of expending energy denying a derogatory label, many young participants incorporated it into their own political identity.
Humour became an instrument of resistance rather than a distraction from it. Memes circulated alongside protest schedules. Satirical artwork travelled together with eyewitness videos. The internet did not merely report the movement. It actively participated in constructing it.
This phenomenon carries profound implications for democratic politics.
Language has traditionally been one of the most powerful tools available to governments. Describing protesters as irresponsible, violent, misguided, or anti-national often shapes public attitudes before any investigation into underlying grievances begins.
Labels simplify complex realities. They reduce citizens into stereotypes that are easier to dismiss than to engage.
Digital participation has complicated this strategy. Once a politically - charged word enters online circulation, its meaning becomes remarkably unstable. Users reinterpret it through jokes, graphics, music, animation, and collective storytelling.
The original speaker no longer retains exclusive ownership over the expression. Political authority therefore loses one of its oldest advantages, namely the ability to impose definitions upon public debate.
That reality should concern governments far beyond India. The rapid spread of participatory digital culture means that political legitimacy increasingly depends not only upon policy performance but also upon communicative intelligence.
Public officials accustomed to one-way messaging frequently underestimate how quickly their words may be transformed into symbols of resistance.
Nevertheless, the Delhi episode should not be romantici z ed. The willingness of young people to reclaim ridicule demonstrates creativity, but creativity alone cannot resolve structural problems.
Examination paper leaks, educational inequality, unemployment, and institutional mistrust remain deeply rooted challenges requiring administrative competence rather than rhetorical adaptation. A successful meme cannot replace successful governance.
The police response similarly raises uncomfortable questions regarding democratic proportionality.
Governments unquestionably possess the responsibility to maintain public order, particularly near sensitive institutions such as Parliament. Peaceful demonstrations may sometimes deteriorate into confrontations involving damaged property or injured security personnel. States cannot simply abandon their obligation to ensure safety.
At the same time, democratic governments derive legitimacy not merely from maintaining order but from demonstrating restraint while doing so.
The widespread circulation of images depicting tear gas, baton charges, barricades, and injured protesters inevitably shapes public perception regardless of official explanations.
Modern policing unfolds before countless smartphone cameras rather than behind institutional walls. Every tactical decision becomes part of a broader political narrative.
This is precisely where governments encounter a difficult paradox. Strong police action may temporarily disperse crowds, yet visual evidence of that action often amplifies public attention toward the very grievances authorities hoped to contain.
Social media platforms reward emotionally charged content. Images of confrontation generally travel farther than press briefings describing procedural necessity.
Consequently, contemporary protests increasingly operate within two interconnected arenas. One exists physically on streets, university campuses, and public squares. The other exists digitally across platforms where photographs, livestreams, edited videos, and satirical content compete for attention.
Success in one arena does not automatically guarantee success in the other. Governments may restore traffic flow while simultaneously losing control over the public narrative.
The Delhi protests illustrate how these parallel arenas constantly interact.
A barricade dismantled in the street quickly becomes a symbolic image online. A viral slogan encourages more citizens to participate offline. Official statements trigger fresh rounds of digital reinterpretation. Political communication now resembles an endless feedback loop rather than a sequence of isolated events.
There is another dimension that deserves equal scrutiny. The movement reflected growing impatience among younger citizens who increasingly measure democratic performance through lived experience rather than constitutional promise.
Elections remain essential, but they no longer exhaust expectations of accountability. Young voters seek functioning institutions, transparent recruitment processes, credible examinations, and opportunities proportional to their qualifications.
When those expectations repeatedly collapse, frustration naturally extends beyond individual ministries toward broader questions of governance.
This generational shift helps explain why seemingly technical administrative failures often acquire political significance. Examination irregularities are no longer viewed simply as bureaucratic mistakes. They become evidence of a larger system perceived to be indifferent toward aspiration itself.
In societies where educational achievement represents the primary route to economic mobility, compromised examinations undermine the social contract between citizens and the state.
T he symbolism of the Cockroach Janata Party therefore extends beyond satire. It represents an emerging political language in which identity is negotiated collectively rather than imposed from above.
The movement suggests that ridicule has become an increasingly unreliable instrument of political control because audiences no longer consume official narratives passively. They reshape them, often with astonishing speed and creativity.
Yet this transformation should also encourage reflection among protest movements themselves. Digital visibility can generate extraordinary momentum, but momentum is not the same as institutional change.
Hashtags trend for hours. Governments remain for years. Sustaining democratic pressure requires organi z ation, negotiation, policy proposals, and strategic patience alongside symbolic mobili z ation.
Otherwise, movements risk becoming memorable cultural moments without producing meaningful structural reform.
The Indian government likewise faces an important choice. It may interpret these protests simply as another episode of public disorder requiring administrative management.
Alternatively, it may recogni z e them as indicators of a deeper crisis of confidence among younger citizens. The second interpretation demands considerably greater political courage because it requires acknowledging that dissatisfaction cannot always be attributed to opposition parties or external provocation.
The Delhi confrontation should therefore be understood within a broader international pattern. From university campuses to digital platforms, young citizens increasingly refuse to separate cultural expression from political participation.
Humour, irony, music, visual art, and internet culture have become legitimate vehicles for articulating civic demands. Traditional political observers often dismiss these forms as frivolous because they differ from older methods of mobili z ation. Such dismissal misunderstands the communication habits of an entire generation.
Political participation has never remained static. Earlier generations relied upon pamphlets, posters, underground newspapers, trade union meetings, and public rallies. Today's activists possess smartphones capable of broadcasting events worldwide within seconds.
Their political imagination is shaped by interconnected digital communities rather than isolated local organi z ations. Consequently, symbols travel across borders with unprecedented speed. A protest slogan coined in one country may inspire movements thousands of kilometres away within days.
South Asia illustrates this regional interconnectedness particularly well. Young people in Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, Nepal, and Sri Lanka increasingly observe one another's political experiences through social media rather than conventional news alone.
They borrow slogans, adapt protest tactics, reinterpret symbols, and exchange strategies in real time. National politics remains distinct, but political culture has become increasingly transnational.
This interconnectedness creates opportunities as well as risks. Constructive ideas regarding transparency, accountability, and civic participation can spread rapidly across societies. So can misinformation, conspiracy theories, and polari z ation.
Democratic resilience therefore depends not merely upon technological access but upon strengthening critical thinking, institutional credibility, and public trust. Digital literacy has become as important to democracy as constitutional literacy.
HM Nazmul Alam is an Academic, Journalist, and Political Analyst based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Currently he teaches at IUBAT.

item.title: Protection is a life skill. Why aren’t we teaching it?
item.description:
A few weeks ago, I had the opportunity to facilitate a Young Women's Protection Leadership Bootcamp that brought together 22 young women from different parts of Bangladesh and neighboring countries. Over several days, we discussed leadership, advocacy, protection risks, and the challenges young women face in their communities.
I expected to learn a lot from the participants. What I did not expect was how often I would hear the same sentence: "This happens in my community too."
As we discussed real-life cases from Kurigram, Naogaon, Cox's Bazar, Bhubaneswar in India, Nepal, and elsewhere, the details changed but the stories felt remarkably familiar.
A girl leaving school because she was married off too early. A young woman excluded from community decision-making. A survivor struggling to access support services. A family considering a dangerous migration journey because poverty leaves them with few options. A young activist facing online abuse for speaking out about women's rights.
Violence against women and girls remains one of the most widely reported protection concerns in Bangladesh.
Different places. Different circumstances. Yet the same patterns kept appearing.
What struck me most was that these situations rarely emerged overnight. The warning signs were often visible long before the harm occurred.
Yet many individuals, families, and communities did not recognize them as protection concerns until the consequences became severe.
That realization stayed with me long after the bootcamp ended.
Why do we teach children mathematics, science, and language from an early age, but rarely teach them about protection?
By protection education, I do not mean specialized humanitarian training. I mean helping children and young people understand personal safety, rights, consent, gender equality, online risks, discrimination, help-seeking pathways, and how to recognize and respond to abuse, exploitation, and violence.
These are not advanced concepts reserved for lawyers, social workers, or humanitarian professionals. They are life skills.
Yet many young people grow up without ever learning them.
The consequences are all around us. Bangladesh has made remarkable progress in education, health, and poverty reduction. Yet many protection challenges continue to affect the lives of women and girls.
According to Unicef, Bangladesh still has the highest child marriage rate in Asia, with 51% of women aged 20-24 married before the age of 18.
At the same time, violence against women remains widespread. UN Women reports that nearly three out of four ever-married women in Bangladesh have experienced some form of intimate partner violence in their lifetime.
These figures remind us that legal reforms and economic progress alone are not enough. Prevention must begin much earlier, through awareness, education, and changes in social norms.
Many of these risks are rooted in social norms that children absorb from an early age. In many communities, boys are encouraged to be confident, independent, and outspoken. Girls are often expected to be careful, obedient, and mindful of family reputation. While boys are encouraged to explore the world, girls are often taught to navigate its limits.
These expectations may seem small at first. Over time, however, they influence opportunities, choices, and power. For many girls, this can mean fewer opportunities to continue education, participate in leadership, access services, or make decisions about their own lives. It can also increase their vulnerability to violence, exploitation, and discrimination.
This is precisely why protection education matters.
Protection education cannot eliminate every risk. But it can help people recognize risks before they become crises. It can teach young people how to identify unsafe situations, seek support, understand their rights, challenge harmful norms, stay safe online, and support others facing violence or discrimination.
Most importantly, it can help young people see themselves as part of the solution.
I witnessed this firsthand during the bootcamp. The young women participating were not waiting for someone else to solve the problems affecting their communities. They were analyzing protection concerns, mapping risks, identifying barriers, and developing practical action plans.
They discussed child marriage, trafficking, gender-based violence, climate-related risks, and social exclusion with remarkable insight and determination.
Many had experienced some of these challenges personally. Others had witnessed them in their communities. Yet they were not defined by those experiences. They were transforming experience into leadership.
Too often, young women are viewed primarily through the lens of vulnerability. We describe them as victims, beneficiaries, or people in need of support. While support remains essential, this perspective overlooks something equally important.
Young women are leaders. They are advocates. They are changemakers. When given knowledge, space, and opportunity, they do not simply protect themselves. They help protect others, strengthen community resilience, and contribute to safer and more inclusive societies.
This is why programs that invest in young women's leadership are so valuable. They build confidence, strengthen networks, and create local leaders who can identify risks and drive solutions. However, these opportunities should not be limited to those fortunate enough to participate in specialized workshops.
Protection education should become part of how we educate and prepare all young people for life. Protection education does not require a new subject in the curriculum. It can be integrated into existing lessons through discussions on rights, gender equality, digital safety, consent, safe migration, bullying prevention, and help-seeking mechanisms.
Schools, families, community organizations, and youth groups all have a role to play. We teach children how to cross a road safely because we want to prevent harm before it happens. Teaching them how to recognize violence, seek help, understand their rights, and protect themselves and others deserves the same priority.
P rotection is not only a humanitarian issue. It is a life skill. And every child should have the opportunity to learn it.
Fariha Hossain is working on humanitarian and refugee issues.

item.title: When growing old means growing invisible
item.description:
While everyone was caught up in the World Cup, this particular story quickly faded from the headlines: The elderly woman found dead in her Mirpur apartment, weeks after she had passed away alone. The real tragedy was not just in her death, but in how she went unnoticed for so long.
Family ties used to be the main source of support in our society, so this kind of invisibility once felt rare. Now, it is happening more often.
A country ageing faster than it admits
Bangladesh often thinks of itself as a young country, but the numbers tell a different story.
Government estimates say about 13 million people, or around 8% of the population, are already over 60. This number is expected to rise above 20 million soon, which will change the country’s health and social care needs in ways that are not yet fully recognized.
At the same time, growing older is now more often linked to long-term illness and dependency, rather than rest and family support. Studies in Bangladesh show that more than half of older adults have several chronic conditions, such as hypertension, diabetes, heart disease, and respiratory problems.
It is a good thing that people are living longer, but without enough support, this becomes a silent crisis.
When the family-based care model starts to weaken
For many years, families in Bangladesh cared for their elderly members. This worked because families were bigger, migration was limited, and everyone lived close enough to help each other every day.
That reality is changing.
Urban growth, migration, and nuclear families are making it harder to care for elders in traditional ways. Adult children often leave for work in other cities or countries, leaving elderly parents behind. Even when families are in the same city, time pressure and economic demands make it difficult to give regular care.
This does not mean families are abandoning their elders on purpose. Instead, there is more distance now -- physically, emotionally, and in daily life.
The tragedy in Mirpur is a clear example of this change, but it is not a rare case.
Bangladesh’s healthcare system is still largely set up for short-term problems, such as treating sudden illnesses or hospital visits. It is not as prepared to handle the long-term needs of ageing, such as ongoing diseases, gradual decline, disability, and end-of-life support.
There is little organized monitoring for elderly people who live alone. Community support is scattered, and families often have to deal with illness without much help or advice from medical professionals.
Research shows that over 90% of older adults in Bangladesh have health problems that need medical care. This often means they go to the hospital many times, which increases costs for their families.
This is why palliative care becomes central.
Many people think palliative care is only for the end of life, but it is more than that. It aims to improve the lives of people with serious or long-term illnesses by managing pain, providing emotional support, and coordinating care.
The World Health Organisation estimates that tens of millions of people worldwide require palliative care each year, yet most in low- and middle-income countries do not receive it.
Bangladesh is part of this gap.
With chronic diseases rising fast and hospitals already full, palliative care is not a luxury in Bangladesh. It is a vital part of the health system that is still missing.
The hidden cost of neglect
When adequate care systems are absent, the burden does not disappear but shifts.
Families are the first to feel the cost. In many homes, women take on most of the caregiving, often cutting back on work or leaving their jobs to care for older relatives.
The healthcare system also feels the strain. Many older patients go to the hospital for problems that could be managed at home or in the community, which contributes to overcrowding and makes already-busy hospitals less efficient.
There is also a human cost that is harder to see. Loneliness in older adults is more often linked to depression, memory problems, and worse physical health. In busy cities, people often notice this isolation only when a crisis happens.
Why invisibility is the real problem
The Mirpur case makes us think about something uncomfortable. It is not just about one person not being found in time. It shows how easily older people can become invisible in today’s cities.
Cities like Dhaka are crowded, but being close to others does not mean older people are seen. Elderly people living alone can go unnoticed for days. In rural areas, migration has created another kind of distance, in which care is expected but not always provided.
Growing old in Bangladesh now often means being physically close to others but receiving insufficient social attention.
What needs to change
The solutions are not new or complicated. What we need is to bring them together, not invent something entirely different.
Palliative care can be added to basic healthcare services. Community health workers can learn the basics of caring for older people. Local groups can find elderly people living alone and check on them regularly. Home-based care, run by public, private, and NGO partners, can offer ongoing support when hospitals cannot.
Just as important, caregiving should be seen as a responsibility for everyone, not just something families handle quietly on their own.
Other countries that have adopted these systems have seen improved quality of life, fewer hospital visits, and greater dignity at the end of life.
The woman who died alone in Mirpur should not be just another sad news story. Her experience shows a bigger change that is already happening.
Bangladesh is ageing and the question is whether growing old in this country will ever mean care, dignity, and being seen, or quietly fading away.
Shafiq R Bhuiyan writes on how communication, culture and corporate social responsibility (CSR) converge to shape a more conscious and compassionate society.

item.title: Messi lands in Argentine hometown after World Cup defeat
item.description:
Argentina's defeated football hero Lionel Messi returned to his hometown on Tuesday after a painful World Cup final loss.
The national squad captain landed at Rosario airport on a private jet at around 6:30 am (0930 GMT) along with his wife and three children, a local government source told AFP on condition of anonymity.
A video published by sports outlet ESPN showed a gray SUV carrying Messi entering a gated community in the city of Funes.
The house he owns in this suburban area is where he usually stays during visits to his native Rosario in central Argentina.
Most national squad players and their coach Lionel Scaloni arrived in Buenos Aires on Monday night, where thousands of fans enveloped them in cheers, chants, flags and tears.
Argentina lost the World Cup final to Spain 1-0, with soccer idol Messi breaking down in tears after Sunday's defeat.
The 39-year-old star scored eight goals during this year's tournament.

item.title: FIFA opens probe into World Cup final clash between Spain and Argentina
item.description:
FIFA has opened an investigation into the scuffle involving players and coaching staff from Spain and Argentina after Sunday's World Cup final.
The governing body said it has appointed an investigator under Article 36 of the FIFA Disciplinary Code after reviewing the referee's report.
"Following an assessment of the match report from the FIFA World Cup final between Spain and Argentina, disciplinary proceedings have been opened," FIFA said in a statement.
It said the disciplinary committee would decide on the next steps after receiving the investigator's report.
Spain beat Argentina to lift the World Cup, but celebrations after the final whistle gave way to a confrontation involving players from both teams and members of Argentina's coaching staff.
Videos shared on social media showed Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes arguing with Spain defender Eric Garcia before appearing to punch him, setting off a melee.

item.title: Chelsea sign Rogers for reported 157m UK record fee
item.description:
Chelsea signed England midfielder Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa on Tuesday in a deal British media valued at £117 million ($157 million), a price that smashed the transfer record for a British player.
"The 23-year-old forward has signed a contract at Stamford Bridge until 2033," the London club posted on their web site.
Rogers passed a medical on Monday following his return from the World Cup in North America.
"I'm so excited," said Rogers. "For me, Chelsea are the biggest club in London and a club I've always admired since I was a kid," Rogers was quoted as saying by the club.
"I'm really excited about the project with the new manager, the players we've got and where the club is heading. That's why I'm here and I can't wait to get started."
The transfer surpasses the previous record fee for a British player set by Manchester City when they signed England midfielder Elliot Anderson from Nottingham Forest for £116 million earlier in July.
Rogers is the most expensive signing in Chelsea's history, eclipsing the £107 million paid to sign Enzo Fernandez from Benfica in 2023.
The swoop is a significant statement of intent from Chelsea, who convinced Rogers to leave Villa even though -- unlike his former club -- the west Londoners will not play in the Champions League in the coming season.
Chelsea had been chasing Rogers for two years and beat Arsenal to his signature after the Premier League champions refused to match the eye-watering fee demanded by Villa.
Rogers' departure is another blow for Villa boss Unai Emery after Youri Tielemans' move to Manchester United and Lucas Digne's expected switch to Paris Saint-Germain.
"A player with impeccable behaviour and commitment, Morgan leaves Aston Villa with the best wishes of everyone at the football club for both his service to the club and for his future career," said Villa on their website.
Championship side Middlesbrough will receive 20 percent of the fee due to a sell-on clause in the deal when they sold Rogers in Villa in 2024.
Rogers scored 21 goals in 85 league appearances for Villa and was a key figure in their Europa League final victory over Freiburg in May.
- 'Cold' celebration -
He enjoyed a breakout campaign last season, netting 14 times and producing 11 assists in 55 appearances.
"He will always remain a core part of our recent great moments and memories," said Villa.
Chelsea's new manager Xabi Alonso will have to find a way to fit Rogers, Cole Palmer, Pedro Neto, Estevao Willian and another close-season signing Geovany Quenda into his attacking midfield positions.
Following Rogers' arrival at Stamford Bridge, Argentine winger Alejandro Garnacho is expected to be sold by Chelsea before the transfer window shuts.
Rogers is close friends with Palmer after their time together in Manchester City's youth academy.
Palmer's famous 'cold' celebration was inspired by Rogers, who first struck the pose as a Middlesbrough player.
Rogers' signing shows Chelsea can still attract top-class signings despite their failure to qualify for Europe after a dismal 10th place finish in the Premier League last season.
Rogers will link up with Chelsea after taking a break following his role in England's run to the World Cup semi-finals.

item.title: La Liga chief says FIFA 'destroying football industry'
item.description:
The president of the Spanish football league, Javier Tebas, accused FIFA of acting "irresponsibly" following the announcement of discussions regarding a possible 64-team World Cup in 2030, in an interview with an Italian sports daily published Tuesday.
Tebas also said that FIFA president Gianni Infantino's time was "over", telling La Gazzetta dello Sport that there is a "system that is fundamentally flawed", which has allowed him to lead football's global governing body for a decade.
"The football industry is not just about the World Cup, however important it may be," he said.
"They are destroying the football industry -- which generates tens of thousands of jobs -- for an event that lasts 40 days and involves only a minority of players."
At the World Cup opening ceremony in June, Infantino mentioned "discussions about expanding to 64 teams" for the World Cup's centenary in 2030, which will be co-hosted primarily by Spain, Portugal and Morocco, with Paraguay, Uruguay and Argentina also welcoming some matches.
"We have repeatedly expressed our concerns about the competition calendar. And now they want to organise a 64-team World Cup," Tebas added, emphasising that "it is the domestic leagues that keep this sport alive".
"We need fewer national teams and better protection for domestic football at all levels. They don't realise this and are making decisions irresponsibly," Tebas added.

item.title: Bangladesh beat Nepal to seal women’s kabaddi test series
item.description:
Bangladesh national women's kabaddi team won the five-match bilateral kabaddi test series with one match in hand beating touring Nepal women’s kabaddi team by 34-22 points in the fourth match held on Tuesday at the National Kabaddi Stadium in the capital.
With this triumph, the hosts are leading the series 3-1.
Facing a must-win situation to keep the series alive, Nepal came out with aggressive intent from the opening whistle. The visitors dominated the early exchanges and raced to an 8-4 lead in the first half.
However Bangladesh quickly reduced the gap with a series of valuable bonus points before taking control through a combination of effective raids and solid tackles. The home side went into the halftime break with a 13-11 lead.
After the interval, Nepal attempted to stage a comeback, but Bangladesh's disciplined tactical play proved too strong for them. At one stage, Bangladesh executed a crucial super tackle to earn two points, extending the lead to 21-15.
Later, Meby Chakma produced a brilliant super raid, adding three more points to put the hosts in commanding position.
Bangladesh then inflicted an all-out on the visitors, taking complete control of the contest. The home side eventually cruised to a convincing 34-22 victory at the final whistle.
Brishty Biswas of Bangladesh was named the player of the match for her impressive performance in the match.
The last match of the series will be held on Thursday at the same venue.

item.title: The philosophy behind Studio Ghibli’s magic
item.description:
Hayao Miyazaki has spent his entire career drawing worlds that feel more alive than our own.
Yet beneath the flying castles, enchanted forests and talking spirits lies a remarkably simple philosophy: animation should bring people closer to humanity, not further away from it.
For the legendary Studio Ghibli co-founder, imagination has never been an escape from reality. It is a way of seeing reality more clearly.
That belief runs through nearly every film he has made.
His stories are filled with fantasy, but they are grounded in emotions that feel unmistakably real -- fear, wonder, loneliness, compassion and hope.
Miyazaki has often argued that fantasy should expand the human imagination, not replace the world we inhabit.
He has warned that virtual realities risk becoming a denial of reality itself, imprisoning people rather than enriching their lives.
This philosophy is closely tied to what scholars describe as Miyazaki’s “critical animism” -- the belief that nature is not simply a resource for humans to exploit but a living world deserving of respect.
Forest spirits, rivers and ancient creatures are not decorative fantasy elements in his films; they embody the idea that the natural world possesses its own dignity and life.
Whether through the Kodama in Princess Mononoke or the river spirit in Spirited Away, nature becomes a character rather than a backdrop.
That same commitment to authenticity shapes the people who inhabit his stories.
Miyazaki has repeatedly criticised modern animation for relying too heavily on clichés instead of careful observation.
In his view, too many animators draw characters inspired by other cartoons rather than by real human beings.
Genuine emotion, he argues, comes from watching how people move, hesitate, smile and grieve in everyday life. His films feel deeply human because they begin with humanity itself.
Perhaps that is why traditional heroes and villains rarely exist in his work.
Rather than dividing the world neatly into good and evil, Miyazaki fills his stories with flawed individuals trying to navigate complicated situations.
He has said he dislikes narratives that justify killing countless enemies simply because they stand on the opposite side.
Human beings, in his eyes, are morally complex, and his films embrace that complexity instead of simplifying it.
His characters also quietly challenge conventional ideas about gender.
Miyazaki’s heroines are courageous without becoming stereotypes of toughness. They overcome fear through empathy, resilience and self-belief rather than through physical dominance.
Male characters are equally liberated from rigid expectations. Figures such as Howl reject conventional masculinity, suggesting that authenticity matters far more than conformity.
That pursuit of authenticity extends even to the way Miyazaki makes his films.
For decades he insisted that animation begins with a pencil.
While Studio Ghibli has occasionally incorporated digital techniques, Miyazaki has remained sceptical of allowing technology to replace human craftsmanship.
Every hand-drawn frame, he believes, carries traces of the artist’s presence -- something no machine can fully reproduce.
His widely publicised criticism of AI-generated art reflects the same conviction: creativity is not simply about producing images but about expressing human experience.
In Miyazaki’s world, animation is more than entertainment.
It is an act of observation, empathy and care. His films remind us that the most magical stories are not those that help us escape reality, but those that return us to it with greater compassion -- for one another and for the world we share.

item.title: The new reality of motherhood after 35
item.description:
When actress Anne Hathaway announced her third pregnancy on June 19 at the age of 43, fans celebrated the news across social media.
Best known to many as Catwoman and the star of The Devil Wears Prada, Hathaway’s announcement was more than another celebrity milestone.
It also drew attention to a growing global trend: more women are choosing to become mothers later in life.
In obstetric medicine, pregnancy after the age of 35 is referred to as Advanced Maternal Age (AMA).
While many women in this age group experience healthy pregnancies and give birth to healthy babies, the likelihood of certain complications increases as maternal age rises.
As more women delay childbirth for education, careers and financial stability, understanding those risks has become increasingly important.
Hathaway herself has spoken candidly about pregnancy loss. Reflecting on a miscarriage in a 2024 interview with Vanity Fair, she said: “It’s really hard to want something so much and to wonder if you’re doing something wrong.”
Her experience mirrors one faced by many women.
Research has consistently shown that the risk of miscarriage increases with maternal age, particularly during the first trimester.
As women grow older, both egg quality and chromosomal abnormalities become more common, raising the chances of spontaneous pregnancy loss.
Miscarriage, however, is only part of the picture.
A 2025 study comparing pregnancies in women aged 40 and above with those under 40 found significantly higher rates of pregnancy-related complications among the older group.
Nearly three-quarters delivered by cesarean section, while preterm birth, gestational diabetes, preeclampsia and postpartum haemorrhage were all more common.
Researchers also observed a higher incidence of chromosomal abnormalities among babies born to older mothers.
Why does age matter?
Pregnancy places extraordinary demands on the body.
The mother’s heart and blood vessels must adapt to pump substantially more blood to support both the placenta and the growing fetus.
As women age, these physiological adaptations may become less efficient, increasing the risk of complications such as restricted fetal growth and placental problems.
Yet medical experts are careful to emphasise that age is a risk factor, not a certainty.
Many women over 35, and even over 40, go on to have uncomplicated pregnancies, particularly when they receive early prenatal care, regular monitoring and appropriate medical support.
The issue also carries growing relevance for Bangladesh.
For decades, the country’s maternal health challenges centred on early marriage and teenage pregnancy.
But demographic patterns are gradually changing.
Rising levels of female education, greater workforce participation and increasing economic independence are encouraging many women -- particularly in urban areas -- to postpone marriage and their first pregnancy.
Analyses of the Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey similarly show that women with higher education are more likely to delay childbirth.
As motherhood increasingly begins later in life for many women, healthcare systems must adapt alongside these social changes.
Advanced maternal age should not be viewed as a barrier to pregnancy, but as a stage that often requires closer medical attention.
Anne Hathaway’s announcement reminds us that motherhood has no single timeline.
It also underscores an important reality: while many women safely welcome children later in life, informed decisions and quality prenatal care become more important than ever.

item.title: Why your feed makes you curious, but not smarter
item.description:
If algorithms are good at one thing, it is making curiosity feel effortless.
Every time you pause on a post, watch a video twice, like a photo or leave a comment, the platform learns something about you.
It then ranks the available content according to how likely you are to engage with it again.
That is why your feed becomes increasingly familiar: more of what interests you, delivered faster and with greater precision.
But there is a crucial difference between content that keeps you engaged and content that actually educates you.
Algorithms cannot measure whether a post has deepened your understanding.
They can only measure how you responded to it. Likes, shares, comments and viewing time become signals of value, even when the content itself offers little beyond entertainment.
Imagine you are learning the piano.
The algorithm could recommend an advanced lesson on harmony or a short video titled “Three easy piano tricks to impress your crush.”
One is more educational. The other is more clickable.
Most people will choose the second.
That is why social media often creates the sensation of learning without demanding the work that real learning requires.
A feed can introduce you to ideas, terms and subjects, but mastery rarely comes from material designed to be consumed in seconds.
Psychologist Robert Bjork used the phrase “desirable difficulties” to describe the effortful conditions that strengthen long-term learning.
Genuine growth often feels slow, uncomfortable and demanding.
Social media usually offers the opposite: instant clarity, quick reward and no requirement to struggle.
Still, algorithms are remarkably effective at sparking new interests.
Because they cannot predict exactly what will capture your attention at a particular moment, platforms constantly vary the subjects, creators and formats appearing on your feed.
One day, you may know almost nothing about astronomy.
Then a post about “diamond rain” on Jupiter appears, and suddenly the solar system becomes fascinating.
But the purpose of this variety is not necessarily to enrich you. It is to keep you watching.
The algorithm may move you across music, psychology, neuroscience, history and countless other subjects.
What it rarely does is move you upward through increasing levels of difficulty.
You may explore many hills without ever climbing a mountain.
Even when you repeatedly engage with the same subject, the content served to you often remains simple, attractive and easy to digest.
Our instincts naturally pull us towards what feels effortless, and algorithms are designed to reinforce that preference rather than challenge it.
This becomes a problem because attention is limited.
The more of it spent scrolling, the less remains for reading, practice, reflection and sustained concentration -- the activities required for real improvement.
Social media can open a door. It can introduce a subject, trigger curiosity and help people discover passions they did not know they had.
But it cannot do the difficult work on their behalf.
The next time TikTok, Instagram or Pinterest sparks a new interest, resist the urge to keep scrolling indefinitely.
Read the books. Practise the skill. Study beyond the headline.
Your feed can introduce you to a subject.
Only effort can teach it to you.

item.title: The complicated life behind Eat, Pray, Love
item.description:
For years, Elizabeth Gilbert built one of the world’s most recognizable brands around healing, authenticity and self-discovery.
Through bestselling books such as Eat, Pray, Love, Committed and Big Magic, she encouraged millions of readers to embrace vulnerability, seek personal freedom and pursue lives guided by honesty rather than expectation.
Her latest memoir, however, presents a far more unsettling portrait -- one that has left readers questioning not only the author herself but also the philosophy that made her famous.
Eat, Pray, Love chronicled Gilbert’s journey through Italy, India and Indonesia following the collapse of her first marriage, arguing that fulfillment begins with the courage to rebuild one’s life.
Its follow-up, Committed, reflected on her relationship with José Nunes -- fictionalized as Felipe in the earlier memoir -- and their eventual decision to marry after initially rejecting the institution altogether.
Together, the books became a celebration of emotional honesty, commitment and personal transformation.
Life, however, took a dramatically different turn.
At 47, Gilbert ended her nine-year marriage to Nunes after falling in love with her close friend of 15 years, Rayya Elias, a musician recovering from addiction who had been diagnosed with terminal pancreatic cancer.
Gilbert publicly described the relationship as an awakening, choosing to leave her marriage and spend Elias’s final years by her side.
It is that relationship that forms the emotional centre of All the Way to the River.
The memoir recounts the immense strain of caring for a terminally ill partner while navigating addiction, grief and emotional exhaustion.
Gilbert describes allowing Elias to relapse after her cancer diagnosis, providing money when she sought drugs instead of treatment and remaining by her side as addiction increasingly overtook their lives.
As the situation deteriorated, Gilbert eventually asked Elias to leave their shared home. Elias later died following a relapse.
The memoir has sparked intense debate, not only because of what Gilbert reveals but because of how she tells the story.
Elias’s family criticised the book as exploitative, arguing that her death had been turned into a public narrative without sufficient regard for those she left behind.
What has unsettled many readers most is Gilbert’s willingness to expose her own darkest thoughts.
She writes candidly about enabling addiction, her growing resentment as a caregiver and, at one point, fantasies of ending her partner’s suffering -- passages that challenge the carefully cultivated image of the compassionate, spiritually enlightened guide many readers associated with her work.
Rather than offering redemption or moral certainty, the memoir presents a deeply flawed narrator confronting her own contradictions.
Those contradictions inevitably invite readers to reconsider Gilbert’s earlier books.
The writer who celebrated lifelong commitment eventually left the marriage that inspired Committed.
The advocate of authentic living repeatedly rebuilt her identity after profound personal upheavals.
The public figure who encouraged emotional wisdom now reveals moments marked by anger, desperation and moral ambiguity.
Whether those contradictions amount to hypocrisy or simply reflect the complexity of being human is ultimately for readers to decide.
Perhaps that is the uncomfortable lesson Gilbert’s latest work leaves behind.
The people who write about healing are not necessarily healed.
Those who teach others how to find themselves may spend their own lives searching.
The distance between the wisdom an author offers and the life they actually live can be wider than readers imagine -- and sometimes, it is within that gap that the most revealing story emerges.

item.title: How oil became Venezuela’s curse
item.description:
Long before Venezuela’s economic collapse, Venezuelan economist and OPEC co-founder Juan Pablo Pérez Alfonzo issued a warning that sounded almost absurd at the time: “Oil is the devil’s excrement.”
Decades later, those words have come to define one of the greatest economic collapses in modern history.
Venezuela sits atop the world’s largest proven oil reserves -- more than 295 billion barrels, accounting for over one-fifth of global reserves.
For much of the twentieth century, that vast wealth transformed the country into one of Latin America’s most prosperous economies.
Oil exports fuelled rapid growth, attracted foreign investment and turned the state-owned oil company, PDVSA, into the backbone of the national economy.
But prosperity built on a single resource proved dangerously fragile.
When Hugo Chávez took office in 1999, soaring oil prices gave his government unprecedented financial power.
As crude climbed from roughly $10 to more than $60 a barrel, billions of dollars flowed into state coffers.
Chávez used that windfall to finance ambitious social programs, expanding access to education, healthcare, subsidised food and housing.
Poverty fell, and his popularity surged.
Yet the boom concealed deeper weaknesses.
Successive governments poured resources into the oil sector while expanding state control over telecommunications, agriculture, steel and other industries.
Many private businesses closed or left the country, investment slowed and domestic production weakened.
Venezuela became increasingly dependent on imports for food, medicine and everyday consumer goods -- all paid for by oil revenues.
The country’s fortunes became tied almost entirely to a single commodity.
That dependence became even riskier after the 2002 strike at PDVSA, when thousands of experienced engineers and technical staff were dismissed and replaced.
While oil income continued to sustain public spending, institutional capacity steadily eroded.
Corruption flourished, political power became increasingly centralised and critics accused the government of weakening democratic institutions, including the judiciary.
For years, rising oil prices masked those problems.
Then the market turned.
After Nicolás Maduro assumed the presidency following Chávez’s death in 2013, global oil prices collapsed from around $100 a barrel to nearly $30.
Because oil generated about 95% of Venezuela’s export earnings and more than half of government revenue, the shock devastated public finances.
Later US sanctions further restricted the country’s access to international markets, compounding an economy already weakened by years of mismanagement.
The consequences were catastrophic.
Hyperinflation reached an estimated 1.37 million percent in 2018 as the government printed money to finance spending.
Food and medicine became scarce, diseases such as malaria resurged, and millions of Venezuelans fled the country in one of Latin America’s largest migration crises.
By 2021, poverty affected more than 94% of the population by international income standards, while the economy had lost nearly 80% of its output over the previous decade.
Harvard economist Ricardo Hausmann described the scale of the collapse starkly: Venezuela’s economic contraction exceeded twice the size of the Great Depression in the United States.
Venezuela’s tragedy was never a shortage of natural resources. It was the failure to build an economy beyond them.
The country remains a powerful reminder of what economists call the “resource curse,” the paradox in which extraordinary natural wealth becomes a source of vulnerability rather than prosperity.
Without strong institutions, transparent governance and economic diversification, even the world’s richest oil reserves can become the foundation of a national crisis rather than national prosperity.

Jamaat MP's viral video: What people in Satkhira are saying
item.description:
A viral video purportedly showing a "private moment" involving Jamaat-e-Islami Member of Parliament (MP) Gazi Nazrul Islam has sparked widespread discussion and criticism in Satkhira. Gazi Nazrul Islam represents the Satkhira-4 (Shyamnagar) constituency.

Since Monday night, multiple videos of the MP's alleged private moments have been circulating on social media. The clips show Gazi Nazrul Islam in close proximity with a young woman.

Immediately after the videos surfaced, many Jamaat leaders and activists claimed on social media that they were generated using artificial intelligence (AI). However, on Tuesday afternoon, Gazi Nazrul Islam posted on his Facebook account stating that the woman in the videos is his second wife, Mariam Begum. He said they were married on 17 June in a family ceremony at the Dhaka residence of Mariam''s father, Masum Billah, with the consent of his first wife.

The videos have prompted reactions from leaders and activists of both the BNP and Jamaat.

Abu Zahid, member secretary of the Satkhira District BNP, told Prothom Alo by phone, "As an MP and a senior individual, what he has done is deeply shameful. It reflects a complete lack of judgment." He demanded that the incident be investigated.

Shahin Islam, organising secretary of the Satkhira district unit of Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal, said in a video message, "This is very unfortunate. I believe Gazi Nazrul Islam should voluntarily resign from the public office he holds. At the same time, Jamaat should take whatever disciplinary action its party rules require."

Jamaat MP's ‘private moment’ video goes viral, he issues explanation on Facebook

Former Satkhira Town Chhatra Shibir president Al Mamun wrote on Facebook, "So much sacrifice, so much hardship, so many struggles! Alas, you have stained our beloved caravan."

Responding to that post, Mohammad Imadul, former convener of Satkhira pourashava Chhatra Dal, commented, "Thank you, brother, for speaking the truth. Such individuals deserve the highest punishment."

In the comments section of Al Mamun''s post, Abdul Al Mamun, a Jamaat supporter, wrote, "Brother, now it seems we have no choice but to stay behind closed doors."

Khalid Hasan, identified as a Chhatra Shibir activist, commented, "We should set an example by ensuring exemplary punishment to show that we do not condone members of our own organisation."

Masudul Alam, president of the Satkhira Government College unit of Chhatra Dal, wrote, "Let's see whether Jamaat stays true to its principles."

Another commenter, Ruhul Amin, wrote, "Since this afternoon, I feel as though both my arms and legs have been paralysed after seeing this news."

Expressing disappointment, one Naeem Shahadat commented on Al Mamun''s post, "I will not comment on whether the woman is indeed his second wife. I will only say that you have caused enormous damage to Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami."

Many other residents of Satkhira have also been sharing their views about the incident on Facebook, with the issue triggering heated exchanges, criticism, and condemnation across social media.

item.title: Social participation essential to prevent hepatitis
item.description:
Around 10 million (1 crore) people in Bangladesh are living with hepatitis B and hepatitis C. Bangladesh is among the 10 countries with the highest number of hepatitis-related deaths worldwide.

The country remains far behind in achieving the goal of eliminating hepatitis by 2030. Participants at a roundtable discussion said that achieving this target will require broad social participation.

These observations emerged at a roundtable discussion titled “Hepatitis: Social Participation is essential for prevention and control”, held yesterday, Tuesday, at the Prothom Alo office in Karwan Bazar, Dhaka.

The Hepatology Society of Dhaka, Bangladesh, and Prothom Alo jointly organised the event ahead of World Hepatitis Day, observed on 28 July.

Speaking as the chief guest, Professor Foara Tasmim, additional director general (Planning and Development) at the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), said, "We cannot solve the hepatitis problem through treatment alone. We must ensure that people do not contract the disease in the first place. We need to raise public awareness, encourage people to protect themselves from infection, and ensure treatment for those who become infected."

She added that the DGHS has prioritised hepatitis prevention and is discussing expanding vaccine coverage and ensuring an adequate vaccine supply with Gavi.

At the beginning of the discussion, Mohammad Saiful Islam, associate professor in the Department of Liver Diseases at Bangladesh Medical University and Scientific Secretary of the Hepatology Society, cited findings from a study showing that 8.5 million (85 lakh) people in Bangladesh are infected with the hepatitis B virus.

Of them, 5.7 million (57 lakh) are men and 2.8 million (28 lakh) are women. Among women of reproductive age between 18 and 45 years, around 1.8 million (18 lakh) are living with the infection, while approximately 400,000 children are affected.

Nearly 1.5 million (15 lakh) families in Bangladesh have at least one member infected with the hepatitis B virus.

Mohammad Saiful Islam said that around 2.5 million (25 lakh) job seekers and working-age people aged 15 to 30 years are infected with hepatitis B.

He noted that many employers automatically declare hepatitis B-positive candidates ineligible for employment, adding, "This is not a scientifically justified practice."

The event also highlighted that several types of hepatitis viruses exist, including hepatitis A, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, hepatitis D, and hepatitis E, each causing different forms of the disease. Hepatitis C is a leading cause of liver cirrhosis and liver cancer.

Ten countries account for 69 per cent of hepatitis C-related deaths worldwide, including China, India, Bangladesh, Indonesia, Nigeria, Ethiopia, Ghana, the Philippines, South Africa, and Vietnam.

Mohammad Kamrul Anam, physician at the National Institute of Gastroenterology and Liver Diseases and Hospital and International Affairs Secretary of the Hepatology Society, emphasised the importance of screening and vaccination to prevent hepatitis transmission.

He said that all adults living in areas with a high prevalence of hepatitis B should undergo hepatitis testing at least once in their lifetime.

He added that people with liver disease, individuals with weakened immune systems, people who use or previously used injectable drugs, prisoners, patients undergoing dialysis, blood or organ donors, healthcare workers, and pregnant women should all undergo hepatitis screening. He then explained the methods used for hepatitis screening and diagnosis.

Tanvir Ahmad, assistant professor at Bangladesh Medical University and Media and Publications Secretary of the Hepatology Society, said that hepatitis is preventable, detectable, treatable and, in many cases, can be eliminated.

He said that the Hepatology Society organises education and training programmes, workshops, scientific seminars, and conferences for physicians.

He also said that the organisation plans to expand nationwide awareness campaigns, conduct targeted screening among high-risk populations, introduce awareness programmes in educational institutions, and strengthen international collaboration.

SAM Nazmul Hasan, associate professor in the Department of Liver Diseases at Bangladesh Medical University and Organising Secretary of the Hepatology Society, said the media has five key responsibilities: presenting science-based information; promoting preventive behaviour; encouraging people to undergo screening; highlighting fear, stigma and social discrimination; and playing a constructive role in shaping public health policy.

Professor Abdullah Al Mahmud, head of the Department of Liver Diseases at Chattogram Medical College and Founding President of the Liver Care Society, said Bangladesh has been administering the hepatitis vaccine through the Expanded Programme on Immunisation (EPI) since 2003.

He said everyone born before 2003 should undergo hepatitis screening. He added that surveys have found hepatitis infection rates ranging from 1 to 5 per cent among various occupational groups in Chattogram, including students, salon workers and hospital technicians.

Professor Ruknuzzaman, chairman of the Department of Pediatric Gastroenterology at Bangladesh Medical University, said hepatitis A and hepatitis E spread primarily through contaminated food.

He noted that street food is one of the major sources of these infections. He added that the hepatitis vaccine effectively protects people against liver cancer and therefore may also be regarded as a cancer-preventing vaccine.

Professor Firoza Begum, president of the Obstetrical and Gynaecological Society of Bangladesh (OGSB), said hepatitis B and hepatitis C are among the leading causes of chronic diseases such as liver cirrhosis and liver cancer.

She explained that these viruses spread from mother to child as well as from one infected person to another. Transmission from mother to newborn usually occurs during childbirth. She said newborns should receive the hepatitis vaccine within 12 hours of birth to prevent infection.

Speaking about the history and significance of World Hepatitis Day, Professor Mohammad Golam Azam, general secretary of the Hepatology Society and Head of the Department of Liver and Gastroenterology at BIRDEM General Hospital, said fatty liver disease can lead to hepatitis. He added that alcohol consumption and certain tuberculosis medications may also cause hepatitis.

In his closing remarks, Professor Mohammad Shahinul Alam, chairman of the Department of Hepatology at Bangladesh Medical University and president of the Hepatology Society, said, "The greatest obstacle to preventing or eliminating hepatitis is ignorance and a lack of awareness. Ninety per cent of infected people do not even know that they carry the virus. Around 8.5 million (85 lakh) people in Bangladesh are infected with hepatitis B, while another 1.5 million (15 lakh) are living with hepatitis C. However, treatment is available, and effective medicines exist."

He added, "Preventing and controlling hepatitis requires social participation. Social participation means the involvement of all stakeholders, including physicians, the government, the state, the media, professional organisations and researchers."

Firoz Choudhury, assistant editor of Prothom Alo, moderated the roundtable discussion.

item.title: India presses China to tackle issues of market access, trade balance
item.description:
ASEAN-PHILIPPINES/

Indian foreign minister S Jaishankar said on Wednesday he told Chinese counterpart Wang Yi that the neighbours should tackle key aspects of relations, such as fair market access and trade balance, in New Delhi's effort to repair ties with Beijing.

Relations between the nuclear-armed nations improved in 2024, ending years of ‌friction dating from a border clash in 2020, after talks between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping in October 2024.

"There are also concerns about predictability of supply chains ... We also need to agree on the meetings of various mechanisms and platforms as per our mutual priorities," Jaishankar said on X.

"Peace and tranquility in the border areas is obviously the prerequisite for normal ties," Jaishankar added after the meeting, held on the sidelines of a regional gathering in the Philippine capital of Manila.

"Since October 2024, both sides have engaged to ensure that important objective. This will continue to need our constant attention."

India and China have resumed direct flights and New Delhi has cut red tape to speed up approvals of business visas for Chinese professionals since October 2024.

Both will also resume border trade from 1 August, following a six-year gap, domestic media said.

India’s $132 billion worth of imports from China in fiscal year 2025/26 were its highest from any nation, with a deficit of more than $100 billion in their total trade of $151.10 billion.

India, which imports inputs and machinery critical for its factories, eased curbs this year on Chinese investments in some industries, a major step towards ​rebuilding ties with Beijing.

In 2020, New Delhi tightened scrutiny of investments from Chinese companies, ​as relations soured after their troops clashed on their largely undemarcated Himalayan frontier, killing 20 Indian and four Chinese soldiers.

At least 26 people have died this week in India's northeastern state of Assam due to flooding after incessant rain, authorities said, with more thunderstorms and strong winds expected to hit several parts of the country's north and east on Wednesday.

The Assam disaster management authority said 21 people were killed on Tuesday, after severe flooding in the state, bringing the week's total to 26.

The Brahmaputra, one of the world's largest rivers, was above its danger mark in some places, authorities said. The state sees damage from the increased flow of water nearly every year during monsoon.

The key Jammu-Srinagar highway was closed to vehicles after multiple mudslides, the Jammu and Kashmir traffic police said in a post on X.

The Kedarnath pilgrimage was suspended in some areas on Wednesday and pilgrims taken to safe areas after boulders and rocks fell on the route, ANI news agency reported.

India's weather office forecast more heavy rain and thunderstorms for Assam, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh and Jammu and Kashmir in the north on Wednesday.
